
# Initialize and Configure OpenSpec

## Learning objective

This chapter walks through installing OpenSpec 1.13.1 and configuring both repositories with
project context that the team can review and maintain in version control.

## What initialization adds

When you initialize a repository, OpenSpec generates GitHub Copilot integration files from a
selected profile.  These files can keep repository-specific constraints close to the code they
govern and make the configuration visible in version control.  That makes them a reasonable
place to start, although the generated profile may still need repository-specific review.

## Install and inspect the CLI

You can install the pinned OpenSpec package with npm.  It is worth checking that the CLI reports
version 1.13.1 and inspecting the available commands before initializing either repository.

It helps to keep two maintenance actions separate:

- Upgrade the package when the team changes the OpenSpec CLI version.
- Run `openspec update` when the team needs to refresh repository integrations from the installed
	package.

## Configure the backend repository

In the backend repository, you can initialize GitHub Copilot support with the profile that covers
Java, Spring Boot, Maven, JPA, H2, testing, and OpenAPI ownership.  Before committing the
generated files, review them to see whether the repository-specific rules describe the backend
rather than the frontend.

## Configure the frontend repository

In the frontend repository, you can initialize GitHub Copilot support with the profile that
covers Angular, the generated client, Vitest, component tests, and Playwright.  Backend
implementation rules generally belong in the backend repository.  The frontend consumes the
backend contract, but it does not own the backend implementation.

## Hands-on exercise: initialize both repositories

You can use the parallel VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA instructions to initialize and configure both
repositories.  Performing the same repository operations in each IDE may help distinguish an IDE
integration problem from an OpenSpec configuration problem.

## Verification checkpoint: inspect the result

For a newly initialized repository, consider running the version, status, validation, and health
checks that apply.  These checks should let you confirm that:

- the CLI reports OpenSpec 1.13.1;
- each repository has the expected generated integration files;
- validation accepts the generated configuration; and
- the health check reports a usable initialization.

Reviewing the generated diff before committing can show what initialization added.  The
repository instructions can then remain the team-owned description of local constraints.

## What you learned

OpenSpec generates the integration files, while the team can retain ownership of the
repository-specific constraints and their review.  When the CLI version changes, the team can
upgrade the package.  When it needs to refresh integrations from the installed version, it can run
`openspec update`.
